text: This is where the agreed definition becomes real, testable T-SQL. One query against Northfield's database that returns exactly one row per customer, classified Active, Churned, or Not Yet Retained.
It starts with a declared variable instead of a hardcoded current-date function buried inline, so the same query can be re-run against any historical date for testing.

Two CTEs do the heavy lifting. One resolves each customer's last qualifying purchase date, filtering out returns and refunds by requiring a positive order total. The other counts purchases in the trailing twelve months.

Both CTEs join back to the customer dimension with LEFT JOINs, so customers with zero orders still appear, and a CASE expression classifies each one, mirroring the earlier addendum exactly, with wholesale accounts filtered out in the base WHERE clause.

Before trusting it, run a sanity check. Group the result by status and look at the counts. If churned comes back at zero, or at nearly the entire customer base, the date math has a bug. Don't move on until the distribution looks plausible.
The foundation query is written and checked. Next: bringing this data into Power BI and shaping it into a real model.
